Maladaptive Strategies.value: ruminate about how event could have been prevented
go over and over why the event happened to me
rehearse what to say before any interaction

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

vignette: Mele was a 75-year-old Samoan woman who had spent most of her life in her homeland before moving to the United States with her husband. As an auditor, she had always been meticulous and detail-oriented, but after surviving a brutal civil war in her home country, Mele's life began to unravel. The memories of that time were etched vividly in her mind - the sound of gunfire, the smell of sweat and smoke, and the sight of destruction all around. When she caught a whiff of body odor or sweat, it transported her back to those chaotic days, and she would feel herself slipping into a daze (Triggers -> Memory). Mele couldn't shake off the feeling that others could see right through her, that they knew what had happened to her just by looking at her (Exposed to Others). She felt like she was living in a constant state of vulnerability. As she navigated her daily routine, Mele would often find herself rehearsing conversations before interacting with anyone, from coworkers to family members. It was as if she needed to script out every possible scenario to avoid any potential pitfalls (Rehearse Conversations). She couldn't explain why this had become such a compulsive habit, but it made her feel slightly more in control. When Mele was at work, the fluorescent lights overhead would sometimes remind her of the harsh sunlight that beat down on her during those long days hiding from gunfire. The familiar hum of the office equipment would give way to the sounds of chaos and panic (Triggers -> Memory). Her colleagues might notice a far-off look in her eyes, but Mele was lost in a world of memories. Mele's memories were fragmented and disjointed, like looking at old photographs scattered across a table. She could see images from that time, but couldn't quite string them together into a coherent narrative (Photographic Recall). The smell of smoke would waft through her mind, carrying with it the acrid taste of fear (Olfactory Recall). Feeling happy or relaxed was no longer an option for Mele; every moment of peace felt like a betrayal of those who had suffered. Whenever she found herself smiling or laughing, she'd be overcome with guilt and quickly shut down (Feeling Happy -> Negative Appraisals). Life didn't seem worth living anymore; what was the point when you couldn't escape the darkness that lurked within? At home, Mele's husband would sometimes find her staring blankly at a wall, lost in thought. He'd try to bring her back to reality with gentle words and gestures, but Mele felt like she was trapped in this never-ending cycle of rumination (Rumination: Prevention). Why had they been targeted? What could they have done differently? Mele began to feel like she was walking on eggshells, constantly checking over her shoulder for potential threats. She'd position herself with her back against a wall, scanning the room for any signs of danger (Back to Wall). Taking too many risks became a way for Mele to cope - it was as if she needed to prove to herself that she could still feel something, anything. As the days turned into weeks, and the weeks into months, Mele's world began to shrink. She stopped going out with friends or engaging in activities she once loved. Her marriage suffered, too; her husband felt helpless watching his wife slip further away from reality. It was then that Mele realized she needed help - not just for herself but for those around her who were suffering as well. Mele's memories of the war still lingered, refusing to be silenced. They haunted her every step, every waking moment. Yet, it was in acknowledging this pain that Mele began to see a glimmer of hope - perhaps she could learn to live with these ghosts and find some semblance of peace.
